blocks.content: Locks and semaphores help us solve one problem: correctness. They ensure that multiple threads do not corrupt shared data by accessing it at the wrong time.
However, once correctness is achieved, a new class of concurrency problems appears. The data remains perfectly safe, but some threads stop making progress.
These issues are often more difficult to debug than race conditions because the application does not crash, throw exceptions, or produce incorrect results. Instead, it simply appears stuck.
The three most common progress-related problems are deadlock, livelock, and starvation.
1. The One-Sentence Difference
Although all three involve a lack of progress, the reason behind the failure is different.
In a deadlock, threads are completely blocked because each thread is waiting for a resource held by another thread.
In a livelock, threads are actively running and responding to each other, but their actions continuously prevent any useful work from being completed.
In starvation, the system as a whole continues to run, but one unlucky thread keeps getting denied the resources it needs and never gets a chance to proceed.
A simple way to remember them is:
["Deadlock: Nobody moves.","Livelock: Everybody moves, but nobody gets anywhere.","Starvation: Everyone else moves, but one thread never gets a turn."]
items: Deadlock: Nobody moves.
Livelock: Everybody moves, but nobody gets anywhere.
Starvation: Everyone else moves, but one thread never gets a turn.

blocks.content: 2. Deadlock
A deadlock occurs when two or more threads are waiting for resources held by each other, creating a dependency cycle that can never be resolved.
Each thread is blocked, waiting for something another thread owns. Since no thread can proceed, no thread can release its resource, and the entire system becomes permanently stuck.
The threads are not consuming CPU time. They are simply waiting forever.
The Four Conditions Required for Deadlock
blocks.text: The Four Conditions Required for Deadlock

blocks.content: A deadlock can only occur when all four of the following conditions exist simultaneously.

["Mutual Exclusion: The resource can be held by only one thread at a time. A lock naturally satisfies this condition because only one thread can own it.
","Hold and Wait: A thread already holding one resource continues to hold it while waiting for another resource.
","No Preemption: A resource cannot be forcibly taken away from a thread. The thread must voluntarily release it.
","Circular Wait: A cycle exists where each thread waits for a resource held by another thread in the cycle.
"]
items: Mutual Exclusion: The resource can be held by only one thread at a time. A lock naturally satisfies this condition because only one thread can own it.
Hold and Wait: A thread already holding one resource continues to hold it while waiting for another resource.
No Preemption: A resource cannot be forcibly taken away from a thread. The thread must voluntarily release it.
Circular Wait: A cycle exists where each thread waits for a resource held by another thread in the cycle.

blocks.content: This is the condition that usually creates the deadlock.
How Deadlock Happens
Imagine two locks: Lock1 and Lock2.
Thread A acquires Lock1 and then tries to acquire Lock2.
At the same time, Thread B acquires Lock2 and then tries to acquire Lock1.
Now:
["Thread A waits for Lock2.","Thread B waits for Lock1."]
items: Thread A waits for Lock2.
Thread B waits for Lock1.

blocks.content: Neither thread can continue.
Neither thread can release its current lock.
The application is stuck forever.
Both methods look correct when viewed individually.
The bug only appears because they acquire the same locks in the opposite order.
Why Deadlocks Are Difficult to Debug
blocks.text: Why Deadlocks Are Difficult to Debug

blocks.content: Deadlocks often occur only under very specific timing conditions.
The application may run successfully thousands of times before two threads happen to acquire resources in exactly the wrong order.
This makes deadlocks difficult to reproduce and even harder to diagnose in production systems.
Preventing Deadlocks
Deadlocks can be prevented by breaking at least one of the conditions required for a deadlock to occur. The most common techniques are:
Consistent Lock Ordering: Always acquire multiple locks in the same order throughout the entire application. If every thread acquires Lock1 before Lock2, a circular dependency can never form.

Acquire All Resources Together: Obtain every required lock before starting work. If all locks cannot be acquired, release everything and retry later. This prevents a thread from holding one resource while waiting for another.

Use Lock Timeouts: Instead of waiting forever, attempt to acquire a lock for a limited period. If the lock cannot be acquired, release any held resources and retry. This converts a permanent freeze into a recoverable failure.
Hold Fewer Locks: The simplest solution is often architectural. The fewer locks a thread holds simultaneously, the lower the chance of creating a dependency cycle.
In many cases, redesigning the code to avoid nested locking eliminates the entire category of deadlock problems.
3. Livelock
A livelock occurs when two or more threads remain active and continuously respond to each other, but never make any actual progress.

Unlike a deadlock, no thread is blocked or waiting forever. Every thread is running, consuming CPU cycles, and repeatedly retrying its work. However, their actions keep interfering with one another in such a way that none of them can ever complete.
A simple way to think about livelock is:
The threads are moving, but they are not moving forward.
How Livelock Happens
Livelock often appears when threads are designed to be "polite."
Imagine two threads trying to acquire two resources.
To avoid deadlock, each thread follows a strategy:
["Acquire the first resource.","Try to acquire the second resource.","If the second resource is unavailable, release the first resource.","Retry again."]
items: Acquire the first resource.
Try to acquire the second resource.
If the second resource is unavailable, release the first resource.
Retry again.

blocks.content: This sounds reasonable because threads never wait forever.
The problem occurs when both threads perform the exact same actions at the exact same time.
Thread A acquires Resource 1. Thread B acquires Resource 2. Both attempt to acquire the other's resource. Both fail. Both release their resources. Both retry immediately.
The same sequence repeats again and again. Neither thread is blocked. Neither thread crashes. Neither thread completes its work.
The application appears busy, but useful work never gets done.
Why Livelock Is Harder to Detect Than Deadlock
blocks.text: Why Livelock Is Harder to Detect Than Deadlock

blocks.content: Deadlocks are relatively easy to identify because blocked threads appear in thread dumps and diagnostic tools.
Livelocks are different. The threads are continuously running, so monitoring tools show active threads and normal CPU activity.
In some cases, CPU usage may even become unusually high because the threads are constantly retrying. From the outside, the application looks healthy.
Internally, however, no meaningful progress is being made.
If two threads execute this same logic simultaneously, they can repeatedly acquire one lock, fail to acquire the second, release everything, and retry in perfect synchronization.
As a result, both threads remain active forever without completing their work.
Preventing Livelock

Add Randomized Backoff: The most effective solution is to wait for a small random amount of time before retrying. Instead of immediately trying again, each thread pauses for a slightly different duration.
This breaks the synchronization that causes both threads to collide repeatedly.

Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current()
        .nextInt(10, 100));
Once the retries become slightly different, one thread eventually succeeds and the livelock disappears.
Introduce Asymmetry: Livelocks often occur because both threads behave identically. A simple fix is to make one thread behave differently.
For example:
["Thread A always retries immediately.","Thread B always waits before retrying."]
items: Thread A always retries immediately.
Thread B always waits before retrying.

blocks.content: Because the behavior is no longer perfectly symmetric, the endless retry cycle is broken.
Limit Retry Attempts: Instead of retrying forever, set a maximum number of attempts. If the retry limit is reached, switch to a different strategy such as:
["Blocking until the resource becomes available.","Acquiring locks in a fixed order.","Reporting an error."]
items: Blocking until the resource becomes available.
Acquiring locks in a fixed order.
Reporting an error.

blocks.content: This converts an infinite retry loop into a bounded and recoverable situation.

Key Takeaway

In a deadlock, threads are blocked and waiting forever.

In a livelock, threads are actively running but continuously undo each other's progress.

The system looks busy, CPU usage remains high, and yet no useful work is completed.

That is what makes livelock one of the most deceptive concurrency bugs.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 4. Starvation
Starvation occurs when a thread waits indefinitely for a resource because other threads continuously receive access before it does.

["Unlike a deadlock, there is no dependency cycle.
","Unlike a livelock, threads are not repeatedly interfering with one another.
"]
items: Unlike a deadlock, there is no dependency cycle.
Unlike a livelock, threads are not repeatedly interfering with one another.

blocks.content: The problem is simply that one thread keeps getting skipped while other threads continue to make progress.
The resource becomes available again and again, but every time it does, some other thread gets it first.
As a result, the starved thread may wait forever even though the system itself is running normally.
How Starvation Happens
Starvation is usually caused by an unfair scheduling or locking policy.

Imagine a shared resource that becomes free repeatedly. Several high-priority threads are waiting for it, along with one low-priority thread. Whenever the resource becomes available, the scheduler always chooses one of the high-priority threads first.
The high-priority threads continue making progress. The low-priority thread continues waiting.
Eventually, the low-priority thread may never get a chance to run at all. The system is healthy. The resource is available. Work is being completed.
Yet one unlucky thread is permanently ignored.
Common Causes of Starvation

Unfair Locks: Some lock implementations favor recently arrived threads over threads that have been waiting longer. A thread that has already waited for a long time can be repeatedly overtaken by newer arrivals.
Priority-Based Scheduling: Operating systems and thread schedulers often prefer higher-priority threads. If high-priority threads continuously arrive, low-priority threads may never get CPU time.
Resource Contention: When many threads compete for a limited resource, an unfair allocation strategy can cause certain threads to wait indefinitely while others repeatedly succeed.
Example
The following simplified lock implementation uses a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) strategy.
Newly arrived threads are placed at the front of the queue and get served first.
If new threads continue arriving, a thread at the back of the queue can be overtaken indefinitely.
This is starvation.
Fair Lock Solution
A fair lock serves threads in the order they arrived.
The longest-waiting thread is always given the next opportunity to acquire the lock.
Java provides fairness support directly through ReentrantLock.
Passing true enables fairness.
With fairness enabled, threads are served in FIFO order, making starvation much less likely.
Preventing Starvation
Use Fair Locks: A fair lock serves waiting threads in arrival order. Since the longest-waiting thread is always chosen next, a thread cannot be skipped forever.

Use Aging: In priority-based systems, a thread's priority can gradually increase the longer it waits. Eventually, even a low-priority thread becomes important enough to be selected. This technique is known as aging.
Avoid Unnecessary Priorities: Many systems do not actually require strict priority scheduling.
In such cases, a simple FIFO queue is often a better choice because it naturally distributes opportunities fairly among waiting threads.

6. Common mistakes
Mistake 1: Relying Only on Testing: A deadlock may never appear during testing but still occur in production. Prevention should rely on proper lock ordering, not just extensive testing.
Mistake 2: Confusing Livelock with High CPU Usage: In a livelock, threads are actively running but making no real progress. High CPU usage combined with no completed work is a common warning sign.
Mistake 3: Retrying Without Random Delays: If multiple threads retry at the same time using the same delay, they can repeatedly collide and create a livelock. Adding random jitter helps avoid this.
Mistake 4: Assuming Thread-Safe Means Fair: A lock may prevent data corruption but still allow some threads to wait much longer than others. Thread safety and fairness are separate concepts.
7. Quick reference

["Deadlock: Threads frozen in a circular wait, each holding what the other needs. Fix: consistent lock ordering.
","Livelock: Threads actively running but undoing each other's progress via synchronized backoff. Fix: randomized retry delay.
","Starvation: One thread indefinitely denied a resource while others are served normally. Fix: fair (FIFO) locks or priority aging.
","The four deadlock conditions: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait break any one and deadlock becomes impossible.
","Detecting livelock: Look for high, steady CPU usage paired with zero forward progress on actual work not just high CPU alone.
","Correctness vs fairness: A lock can be perfectly correct (no data corruption) and still be unfair (a specific thread can starve). They are separate guarantees."]
items: Deadlock: Threads frozen in a circular wait, each holding what the other needs. Fix: consistent lock ordering.
Livelock: Threads actively running but undoing each other's progress via synchronized backoff. Fix: randomized retry delay.
Starvation: One thread indefinitely denied a resource while others are served normally. Fix: fair (FIFO) locks or priority aging.
The four deadlock conditions: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait break any one and deadlock becomes impossible.
Detecting livelock: Look for high, steady CPU usage paired with zero forward progress on actual work not just high CPU alone.
Correctness vs fairness: A lock can be perfectly correct (no data corruption) and still be unfair (a specific thread can starve). They are separate guarantees.
